Zambia’s Sweeping Import Restrictions Disrupt Supply Chains and Spur Price Rises

LUSAKA—Zambia’s sweeping new import restrictions, introduced in early June and still in force, are sending shockwaves through the country’s supply chains and stoking concerns about rising prices across a broad range of goods. The government’s policy, announced as a temporary measure to support domestic industries and stabilize the kwacha, has placed strict limits on a wide array of imported products, from construction materials and household appliances to packaged foods.

The restrictions, which apply to over 200 product categories, have already begun to reshape the business landscape. Traders at Lusaka’s bustling Soweto Market report dwindling stocks of imported rice, cooking oil, and electronics. “We are struggling to replace items that have sold out,” said Chipo Banda, an electronics retailer. “Prices have gone up by at least 15% in just two weeks.”

The Ministry of Commerce, Trade and Industry defended the policy as necessary for economic resilience. “We are prioritizing local production and aiming to reduce pressure on foreign exchange reserves,” Permanent Secretary Felix Mwanza said at a press conference Tuesday. “We are closely monitoring the impact and will adjust as needed.”

However, analysts warn that the sudden clampdown could have unintended consequences. “While the aim is to protect local industries, the immediate effect is inflation and supply shortages,” said Grace Kalima, an economist at Lusaka Research Group. “Prices for imported goods have surged, and domestic producers cannot yet fill the gap, especially in specialized products.”

The Zambia Chamber of Commerce and Industry has called for a more targeted approach. “Broad restrictions risk harming consumers and small businesses,” the Chamber said in a statement, urging dialogue between the government and private sector.

On the streets of Lusaka, consumers are already feeling the pinch. “I can’t find the baby formula I usually buy,” said mother-of-two Ruth Phiri. “Everything imported is more expensive or out of stock.”

The government has indicated it will review the policy in August, but for now, uncertainty prevails. Importers such as Mufulira Trading have slowed orders, wary of further regulatory changes. With inflation already at 13% year-on-year, economists warn that prolonged restrictions could exacerbate cost-of-living pressures and slow economic recovery.
